title: AP Research
summary: Design a defensible inquiry, choose an ethical method and explain what the resulting evidence can support.
frameworkNote: Checked against the official course page on 15 October 2026 for 2026-27. This is an original five-part research skill sequence, not prescribed units. It supports the course’s inquiry and communication goals but does not conduct research, supply participant data or replace the student’s own paper, presentation, oral defence and teacher-supervised process.

modules.title: Narrow a question to an answerable claim
modules.focus: Define a population, concept and feasible evidence.
explanation: A topic names an area; a research question identifies an uncertainty that can be investigated. “School transport” is a topic. “How do students at one school describe barriers to using the existing bus service?” defines a population and a kind of evidence without pretending to establish a causal effect.

A literature review helps locate what is already known and where a bounded contribution might fit. An absence in a quick web search is not proof of a research gap. Record search terms, source selection and competing findings so the question grows from an accountable reading process.

workedExample.prompt: Revise “Does technology improve education?” into a feasible inquiry.
steps: Specify a setting and outcome, such as how one class uses a particular feedback tool.
Choose a question that the available method can answer, such as reported experiences, and avoid promising a causal learning gain from interviews alone.

misconception.claim: A broad question is more academically ambitious than a narrow one.
misconception.correction: A focused question can support deeper analysis and clearer limits.

questions.prompt: What is missing from “Does exercise help?”
questions.answer: The population, kind of exercise, outcome and timeframe are undefined.
checkpoints: Names at least two missing elements
Connects them to answerability

questions.prompt: Why retain sources that disagree with your expectation?
questions.hint: Think about the credibility of the review.
questions.answer: They reveal competing explanations and prevent the inquiry from being built only on selected supportive evidence.
checkpoints: Recognises alternative explanations
Avoids cherry-picking

questions.prompt: Operationalise 'library access' for a study of opening hours.
questions.answer: Measure hours available outside pupils' lesson times. Define the school and observation period. Acknowledge that hours do not measure transport or physical access.
checkpoints: Measure hours available outside pupils' lesson times.
Define the school and observation period.
Acknowledge that hours do not measure transport or physical access.

questions.prompt: Why is 'nobody has studied my school' insufficient to establish a research gap?
questions.hint: Novel location is not the same as unresolved knowledge.
hints: Novel location is not the same as unresolved knowledge.
Connect the setting to a meaningful question.
questions.answer: A new location alone may repeat a settled question. The researcher must identify an unresolved issue. The school's context should matter to investigating that issue.
checkpoints: A new location alone may repeat a settled question.
The researcher must identify an unresolved issue.
The school's context should matter to investigating that issue.

notes.title: Narrow a question to an answerable claim in depth
paragraphs: Operationalisation connects an abstract concept to an observable measure or interpretive procedure. 'Engagement' might mean attendance, time on task or participants' accounts, and these are not interchangeable. Define the population and timeframe before choosing what evidence is feasible. A literature gap is a specific unresolved question, not merely a topic unfamiliar to the researcher. The project should explain how its question follows from existing work and why its chosen measure can answer it. Narrow scope can produce a useful contribution when the boundaries are explicit.

workedExamples.prompt: Turn 'Does music help study?' into an answerable observational question.
steps: Specify one class, a week and a measurable outcome such as self-reported concentration during independent reading.
Record music use without claiming random assignment.
workedExamples.conclusion: Ask how reported concentration varies with reported music use in that setting; a causal benefit remains outside the design.

flashcards.back: Defining how a concept will be observed.
No; it measures only one possible dimension.
A documented unresolved question in existing work.
It makes claims and evidence requirements explicit.

diagrams.title: From concept to question
diagrams.description: Measurement determines the question a design can answer.

nodes.label: Bounded association
nodes.detail: Reported concentration compared within one class.

modules.title: Choose a method and protect participants
modules.focus: Match the question to evidence and an ethical process.
explanation: Methods answer different questions. Interviews explore accounts and meanings; observations document behaviour in a setting; experiments test a controlled intervention when a suitable design is feasible. A method is not rigorous merely because it produces numbers or uses a familiar label.

Before collecting information from people, follow school and applicable ethics requirements, obtain the required approvals and consent, and minimise identifiable data. Participation must be voluntary. Do not collect sensitive information simply because it might be interesting. Explain recruitment, storage and withdrawal arrangements in language participants can understand.

workedExample.prompt: Plan a fictional interview study of bus-service barriers.
steps: Use neutral prompts such as “Describe your last journey” rather than “Why is the service unreliable?”
Complete the required review and consent process before recruitment, then document how recordings and identifying details will be protected.

misconception.claim: Consent to participate permits any later use of the data.
misconception.correction: Use must remain within the consent and approved research arrangements.

questions.prompt: Why is “How badly did the new system fail?” a weak interview question?
questions.answer: It assumes failure and pushes respondents toward a negative account.
checkpoints: Identifies leading wording
Suggests neutral framing

questions.prompt: Which method better addresses how participants interpret an experience?
questions.answer: Interviews may be appropriate, provided recruitment and analysis are justified for that question.
checkpoints: Matches method to question
Does not claim automatic superiority

questions.prompt: Revise the invented interview prompt 'Why do you dislike the new canteen?'
questions.answer: Ask 'Describe your experience of the new canteen.' Follow with neutral questions about specific features. Allow positive, negative or mixed responses.
checkpoints: Ask 'Describe your experience of the new canteen.'
Follow with neutral questions about specific features.
Allow positive, negative or mixed responses.

questions.prompt: Why should a researcher not promise anonymity while recording names beside interviews?
questions.answer: Names linked to interviews mean the data are identifiable. Confidentiality may describe restricted disclosure. The information sheet must accurately explain handling and access.
checkpoints: Names linked to interviews mean the data are identifiable.
Confidentiality may describe restricted disclosure.
The information sheet must accurately explain handling and access.

notes.title: Choose a method and protect participants in depth
paragraphs: Method choice follows the kind of answer sought. Interviews can explore meanings; observations can document behaviour; surveys can estimate patterns when sampling supports that use. Recruitment affects whose experiences are visible. Ethical planning includes voluntary participation, appropriate consent, confidentiality and realistic arrangements for storing and deleting data under the applicable review process. Anonymity and confidentiality differ: a researcher may know identities while promising not to disclose them. Collect only what the question requires, and avoid designing a method whose promised protections cannot actually be delivered.

workedExamples.prompt: Plan an invented study of how pupils interpret feedback comments.
steps: Use interviews about supplied examples to explore interpretation rather than claiming to measure long-term learning.
Recruit through an approved voluntary process and separate identifying details from transcripts.
workedExamples.conclusion: The design can explain participants' interpretations within its recruitment limits.

flashcards.back: Participants' meanings and accounts.
Restricting disclosure of identifiable information.
Identities are not known or linkable in the relevant data.
Unnecessary identifiers add risk without answering the question.

diagrams.title: Feedback interview design
diagrams.description: Question, evidence and protection must align.

modules.title: Make analysis traceable
modules.focus: Separate raw observations, coding and interpretation.
explanation: A transparent analysis leaves a path from original evidence to the reported finding. In qualitative work, define codes, record examples and explain changes to the coding scheme. In quantitative work, retain variable definitions, missing-data decisions and calculation steps.

An unusual observation is not automatically an error. Investigate it using stated criteria and retain a record of any exclusion. Do not invent missing values, participant quotations or results. A hypothetical example can demonstrate a calculation, but it must remain visibly separate from collected research data.

workedExample.prompt: Three hypothetical journey times are 10, 15 and 35 minutes. Describe them.
steps: Calculate the mean as 60/3 = 20 minutes and the median as 15 minutes.
Explain that the long journey raises the mean; keep it unless a documented error or predefined exclusion rule justifies removal.

misconception.claim: Removing inconvenient data makes a result clearer and therefore better.
misconception.correction: Undisclosed selective removal distorts the evidence and undermines the conclusion.

questions.prompt: Why keep a coding decision log?
questions.hint: Think about how another reader follows the analysis.
questions.answer: It records how categories were defined and revised, making the interpretation traceable to the evidence.
checkpoints: Names traceability
Includes revisions

questions.prompt: For hypothetical values 4, 4 and 10, find mean and median.
questions.hint: Sort the values and calculate the sum.
questions.answer: Mean = 18/3 = 6; median = 4.
checkpoints: Calculates both
Does not erase the larger value

questions.prompt: Two coders classify 'The journey was cheap but slow' differently. How can the record improve?
hints: Clarify whether multiple codes are allowed.
questions.answer: Define cost and time categories. Allow both codes if consistent with the chosen method. Document the revised rule and revisit comparable statements.
checkpoints: Define cost and time categories.
Allow both codes if consistent with the chosen method.
Document the revised rule and revisit comparable statements.

questions.prompt: A measured value is unusually large but has no recording error. May it simply be deleted?
questions.answer: Unusual size alone does not justify deletion. Apply a documented exclusion rule if relevant. Otherwise retain it and explain its influence or a justified sensitivity analysis.
checkpoints: Unusual size alone does not justify deletion.
Apply a documented exclusion rule if relevant.
Otherwise retain it and explain its influence or a justified sensitivity analysis.

notes.title: Make analysis traceable in depth
paragraphs: Traceable analysis preserves a route from raw evidence to the reported claim. Quantitative work needs defined variables, units and documented treatment of missing values. Qualitative coding needs explicit category definitions and examples, with disagreements or revisions recorded. A category can change during analysis if the method permits it, but silent changes make interpretation difficult to assess. Keep anomalous observations visible unless a justified rule excludes them. A clean-looking result is not a reason to remove inconvenient data or conceal uncertainty.

workedExamples.prompt: Invented survey: four ratings are 2, 3, missing and 5. Report the mean responsibly.
steps: Treat missing as unavailable, not zero; the observed sum is 10 across three ratings.
Compute 10/3, approximately 3.33, and report one missing response.
workedExamples.conclusion: The mean describes three observed ratings, with the missing value explicitly retained in the record.

flashcards.front: Should missing data automatically become zero?
flashcards.back: No; missing and measured zero differ.
Definitions and examples for analytic categories.
They may be valid evidence challenging a pattern.

flashcards.front: What does an audit trail preserve?
flashcards.back: The path from data through decisions to claims.

diagrams.title: Missing is not zero
diagrams.description: A reporting decision changes the denominator.

modules.title: Write a conclusion within the design
modules.focus: Distinguish contribution, limitation and causal overreach.
explanation: A conclusion answers the research question at the scale supported by the method. A convenience sample from one school cannot automatically represent all students. An observed association also does not establish causation without a design and assumptions that address alternative explanations.

A limitation should explain its consequence. “Small sample” is less useful than explaining that the sample may miss infrequent experiences or restrict generalisation. A null or mixed result can still be informative when reported accurately. Do not enlarge the claim merely to make the project sound successful.

workedExample.prompt: A hypothetical survey finds that frequent library users report higher confidence.
steps: State the association within the sampled group.
Discuss selection and other explanations, such as already-confident students choosing the library; do not claim that library use caused confidence.

misconception.claim: A project contributes only if its hypothesis is confirmed.
misconception.correction: A carefully bounded negative or mixed finding can refine understanding and future questions.

questions.prompt: Improve the limitation “Only one school was studied.”
questions.hint: Explain what follows from the scope.
questions.answer: The findings may reflect that school’s timetable and transport arrangements, so transfer to other schools requires caution and comparison.
checkpoints: Names a contextual difference
Explains the inference limit

questions.prompt: What separates implication from result?
questions.answer: A result reports what the analysis found; an implication explains what that finding may mean, with appropriate qualifications.
checkpoints: Defines both
Keeps interpretation bounded

questions.prompt: A study finds no clear difference in a small sample. Why is 'the methods are identical' too strong?
questions.hint: Absence of a clear signal has several explanations.
hints: Absence of a clear signal has several explanations.
questions.answer: The sample may lack precision to detect a difference. The observed result does not prove equivalence. Report the estimate and uncertainty within the design.
checkpoints: The sample may lack precision to detect a difference.
The observed result does not prove equivalence.
Report the estimate and uncertainty within the design.

questions.prompt: Turn 'The project was limited by time' into a useful limitation about interviews.
questions.answer: Limited time restricted recruitment to one class. That narrows the range of experiences represented. The conclusion should not be generalised to all pupils without further study.
checkpoints: Limited time restricted recruitment to one class.
That narrows the range of experiences represented.
The conclusion should not be generalised to all pupils without further study.

notes.title: Write a conclusion within the design in depth
paragraphs: A conclusion should answer the research question at the level the design supports. Separate findings, interpretation and implications so that a measured association does not silently become a causal recommendation. Limitations should explain their likely consequence for interpretation: a convenience sample restricts generalisation, while an imprecise measure may blur differences. A small project can make a contribution by clarifying a pattern or revealing an unanswered question. Claiming universal importance is unnecessary when a precise, bounded conclusion accurately reflects what the study established.

workedExamples.prompt: Invented interviews: six volunteers describe clearer instructions after a form redesign. Write a conclusion.
steps: Report the shared perception among these six volunteers.
Acknowledge voluntary recruitment and the absence of a direct error-rate measure.
workedExamples.conclusion: The redesign was perceived as clearer in this sample; reduced completion errors and wider acceptance remain untested.

flashcards.back: The result of the stated analysis.
A qualified account of what a finding may mean.
Generalisation beyond the recruited group.
No; a bounded insight can be useful.

diagrams.title: Conclusion boundaries
diagrams.description: The design limits the claim's reach.

nodes.label: Unmeasured error rate
nodes.detail: A possible implication requiring new evidence.

modules.title: Defend decisions and preserve the research record
modules.focus: Communicate the argument and reflect on revisions.
explanation: An oral defence asks you to explain why you made particular research decisions and what you learned from the process. Prepare a clear chain from question to method, evidence, conclusion and limitation. Memorised confidence cannot substitute for understanding the actual choices.

Use visuals that support the reasoning and label hypothetical material separately from collected evidence. Keep citations close to borrowed ideas and distinguish your contribution from prior work. A revision log can show how feedback changed the project, including decisions you retained and the reasons for retaining them.

workedExample.prompt: Answer “Why did you use interviews instead of a large survey?”
steps: Connect the method to the question: detailed accounts of barriers were needed.
Acknowledge the trade-off: depth was prioritised, while prevalence and broad generalisation remain outside the design.

misconception.claim: Admitting a limitation weakens the defence.
misconception.correction: Explaining a limitation accurately shows that you understand what the design can support.

questions.prompt: What should a methods slide prioritise?
questions.hint: Link design choices to the question.
questions.answer: The evidence sought, recruitment or source selection, analysis approach and the reason these fit the question.
checkpoints: Explains fit
Avoids a disconnected tool list

questions.prompt: How should you answer an unexpected question you cannot resolve?
questions.hint: Maintain the boundary of your knowledge.
questions.answer: State what the evidence supports, identify what remains uncertain and explain what further work would address it.
checkpoints: Does not fabricate
Proposes a relevant next step

questions.prompt: A researcher changed a coding category midway. What should the final record include?
questions.hint: Preserve the original and revised definitions.
hints: Preserve the original and revised definitions.
Show how earlier data were handled.
questions.answer: Record the reason and date of revision. Retain both category definitions. Explain whether earlier material was recoded consistently.
checkpoints: Record the reason and date of revision.
Retain both category definitions.
Explain whether earlier material was recoded consistently.

questions.prompt: Explain a reasonable future study after observing one lunchtime queue for two days.
questions.answer: Observe more days and service conditions. Include relevant variation such as menu or attendance. Use the broader evidence to test whether the initial pattern persists.
checkpoints: Observe more days and service conditions.
Include relevant variation such as menu or attendance.
Use the broader evidence to test whether the initial pattern persists.

notes.title: Defend decisions and preserve the research record in depth
paragraphs: Defending research means explaining why decisions fit the question and what trade-offs they created. It does not require pretending every choice was optimal. Preserve instruments, analysis rules, versions and permitted evidence so that the final account can be checked against the work actually done. Reflection should identify a concrete decision, its observed consequence and a reasoned alternative. When asked about an unsupported extension, distinguish what was measured from what a future study could test. Acknowledging that boundary demonstrates command of the design.

workedExamples.prompt: Answer an invented defence question: 'Why did you observe queues rather than ask whether pupils liked lunch?'
steps: The question concerned waiting time, so timed observations measured the target directly.
Satisfaction surveys would answer a related but different question and could explain experience, not replace the timing measure.
workedExamples.conclusion: Observation matched the outcome while leaving satisfaction outside the project's evidence.

flashcards.front: What should a method defence connect?
flashcards.back: Question, evidence and design choice.
A decision, consequence and justified alternative.
They show what actually changed and when.
State the boundary and a suitable future test.

diagrams.title: Defending the queue measure
diagrams.description: A design choice follows the outcome of interest.
